extracted.intended_audience: architects, students of architecture, and interested general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for designing and judging capitals (capital forms, proportions, decoration, and grouping) and for choosing and shaping arch lines and masonry (lintel, gable, arch, pointed arch). Emphasises structural function, proportion rules, and visual harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital must fulfill its structural purpose (support)
rubrics_metrics.description: “it fails in its own proper purpose, that of support” — listed as one of the three greatest faults of the Early English capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good capital must be able to bear and distribute the weight above it. Designs that undercut or remove bearing surfaces (e.g., dripstone edges that have no bearing power) are structurally defective. The capital is fundamentally an expansion of the shaft's bearing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital must be adapted to its intended function/environment
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is adapted to a purpose to which it can never be put, that of keeping off rain” — second of the three greatest faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt forms that are intended for external weather protection when the shaft is interior or not exposed. Form should follow the actual environmental and functional requirements of the element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital must permit distinct visible decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: “it cannot be decorated” — third of the three greatest faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A capital's contour should admit ornament and be visibly legible; undercut contours that leave the surface barren (making the capital look lathe-turned) are undesirable for expressive decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five determining quantities of capital proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: “These five quantities are: 1. The height of the shaft, a b; 2. Its diameter, b c; 3. The length of slope of bell, b d; 4. The inclination of this slope, or angle c b d; 5. The depth of abacus, d e.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportion of any capital is a function of combinations of these five quantities; changes in any one produce new valid proportions but also limits beyond which proportion becomes ugly or dangerous. Designers must consider interactions among these quantities rather than treating any single dimension in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 1: Slender shafts may have greater abacus projection
rubrics_metrics.description: “The more slender the shaft, the greater, proportionally, may be the projection of the abacus.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given equal height and other fixed dimensions, reducing shaft diameter allows a larger proportional abacus while preserving safety; visually, a slender shaft often requires a more spreading capital. This is a permissive rule: slender shafts need not have large abaci, but may.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 2: Smaller-scale buildings may use larger abacus excess
rubrics_metrics.description: “The smaller the scale of the building, the greater may be the excess of the abacus over the diameter of the shaft.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material cohesion that supports small projecting masses does not scale linearly; an abacus proportion safe at small scale may be unsafe when enlarged. Conversely, an abacus safe at large scale is safer when reduced in scale. Scale affects allowable projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 3: Greater abacus excess requires steeper bell slope
rubrics_metrics.description: “The greater the excess of abacus, the steeper must be the slope of the bell, the shaft diameter being constant.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If abacus projection increases without changing shaft diameter, increase the slope steepness of the bell to provide adequate supporting power; otherwise the projection becomes unsafe. Steepening the bell increases edge-support strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 4: Steeper bell slope allows thinner abacus
rubrics_metrics.description: “The steeper the slope of the bell, the thinner may be the abacus.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A steep bell concentrates strength in its edges, reducing the abacus's role in equalising pressure; therefore on steep bells the abacus may be relatively thin, while shallow bells require thicker abaci to protect weak edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: The rules are permissive (semi‑imperative)
rubrics_metrics.description: “these four rules are all that are necessary for general criticism; and observe that these are only semi-imperative, — rules of permission, not of compulsion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the four laws as guiding permissions: they state what may be done safely or what will generally look correct, not absolute prohibitions. Designers retain choice; the laws indicate safe/visually harmonious options rather than mandatory dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual harmony: match capital spread to shaft slenderness and building scale
rubrics_metrics.description: “The eye always requires, on a slender shaft, a more spreading capital than it does on a massy one, and a bolder mass of capital on a small scale than on a large.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond structural safety, visual perception demands specific proportional relationships. Avoid imposing flat or only slightly expanded capitals on tall/slender shafts — this spoils the effect of a noble building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design must respond to load distribution (weights can alter form)
rubrics_metrics.description: “By the alteration of this weight ... the architect has it in his power to relieve, and therefore alter, the forms of his capitals. By its various distribution ... the slope of their bells and thickness of abaci will be affected also.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitals should be designed in light of how loads are distributed (centres vs. edges, number of shafts bearing load, etc.). Architects can change shaft diameters, bell slopes, abacus thicknesses, and weight distribution to achieve structural and aesthetic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitals may be formed from a single block or in two stones
rubrics_metrics.description: “the strength of the capital will be undiminished if both are cut out of one block ... in others the detached upper stone is a mere representative of the abacus, and is much thinner than the form of the capital requires, while the true abacus is united with the bell.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either a separate abacus or a unified bell-and-abacus block is acceptable; choice depends on scale and harmony. Where the cornice/string course forms an abacus, the design should conceal or integrate the junction appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cornice/string-course as abacus (harmonious integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Fig. XXVII — deep cornice/string-course strong enough to form abaci; Fig. XXVIII — cornice only forms abaci and ceases to receive the same decoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a continuous cornice is strong enough for capital function, let it form the abacus and allow the bell beneath to be deepened and decorated as a capital. If cornice is weak, use it as abacus only and reduce its decorative role to preserve harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouped shafts: use one serviceable abacus; avoid useless small abaci
rubrics_metrics.description: “When two or more shafts are grouped together, their capitals are usually treated as separate, until they come into actual contact ... one abacus serves, in most cases, for all. ... there is evident sacrifice of sound principle in this system, the smaller abaci being of no use.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In clustered shafts prefer a single, serviceable abacus for the group; small nominal abaci that perform no structural role are wasteful and break sound principle. Conceal awkward junctions by decoration only when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital as consolidator of small masonry (may have no projection)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The capital enables all that masonry to act together, and to receive the pressure from above collectively ... thus every large stone set at any important point to reassemble the force of smaller masonry ... is a capital or 'head' stone, whether it project or not.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitals' fundamental role can be fulfilled without outward projection: large stones that collect and transmit forces of rubble or small masonry act as capitals. Do not judge capitals only by their projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital necessity: where concentrated vertical support exists, capitals are required
rubrics_metrics.description: “wherever there is indication of concentrated vertical support, then the capital is a necessary termination. ... wherever shafts ... are employed, for whatever office ... without capitals, there is a defiance of the natural laws of construction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general evaluative principle, any element that indicates concentrated vertical support should be terminated by a capital. Omission of capitals is either barbaric experimentation or a symptom of decline in structural honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish arch line (visible curve) from line of resistance (structural 'moral' line)
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are, therefore, properly speaking, two arch lines. One is the visible direction or curve of the arch ... The other line, which is the line of resistance, or line of good behavior, may or may not be consistent with the outward and apparent curves ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must be aware that the visible arch profile may differ from the theoretical line of resistance determined by loads. Stability requires that the line of resistance remain within the voussoirs; if it approaches the edge or emerges, failure follows. Ensure the voussoirs/masonry include and protect the true line of resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design arch line (direction) and arch masonry (manner) as two distinct problems
rubrics_metrics.description: “there are, therefore, two distinct questions respecting each arrangement: — First, what is the line or direction of it, which gives it its strength? and, second, what is the manner of masonry of it, which gives it its consistence?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First choose an appropriate arch line/curve for the span and loads; then choose voussoir shapes, bonding, and masonry techniques to fortify that line and keep the line of resistance well within the voussoirs under expected load variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose arch type and voussoir strategy according to material and lifting capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification: lintel (single stone), gable (two tilted stones), arch (many voussoirs), and pointed arch (two curves set against each other). “The great value of the arch is, that it permits small stones to be used with safety instead of large ones ... Stones cut into the shape ... are called Voussoirs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select lintel, gable, or arch based on availability and size of stones and on whether large stones can be lifted. Use voussoirs when large monoliths are impractical; cut voussoirs to shapes that interlock and transmit thrust so that many small units act as a stable whole.
